articles.title: DOJ files new charges against 2 ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden case
articles.summary: Washington —  A federal magistrate judge on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department's 11th hour attempt to file new criminal charges against two former FBI counterintelligence officials, saying prosecutors could not take that step without judicial review first. In a tense exchange, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia expressed shock and anger at the Justice Department for filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint against the two FBI officials after midnight on Tuesday on the public court docket, noting it was never reviewed by him to establish where there was probable cause a crime was committed. Filing an unsworn complaint on the public docket and bypassing judicial review, he said, is unheard of and raises questions about the DOJ's motivations. He said he would be ordering that the new version of the charging documents be "struck from the record," though the Justice Department could try to add new charges the proper way. "We have never had complaints filed that are unsigned," Faruqui said. "It is inappropriate. It harms the defendants." "I am unaware of that ever happening before in this court," he added. "I am frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night. But I am much more concerned that it is filed on the public record." John Borchert, a prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., conceded that the effort by the government to add fresh charges without judicial review in a criminal complaint was a first for him as well. He asked if Faruqui would agree to simply agree to let the FBI agent who filed the affidavit in support of the new complaint swear and attest to his filing and then proceed with a hearing to determine if probable cause was met. Defense attorneys for the two ex-officials balked, with one calling such a move "Kafkaesque" and Faruqui analogizing such an action to simply serving as a notary. Faruqui accused the government of repeatedly making bizarre moves in the case that only raise concerns, saying it was like throwing gasoline on a fire, citing how the case was charged and the decision to use a special assistant U.S. attorney from out of town to help prosecute the case. "Everything you're doing is making me more and more concerned," he said.  "Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases? It makes it looks like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause." "Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding," Borchert said. Faruqui said that while he was dismissing the superseding complaint with the new charge of obstructing a congressional proceeding, the court would still proceed with a preliminary hearing to determine whether the original criminal complaint charging them with lying to Congress, which was reviewed by a magistrate judge, meets the probable cause standard. Mary Dohrmann, one of Floris' attorneys, told the court that the changes between the original complaint and the new one the government tried to file were substantial and raised concerns about accuracy. "The evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football, and not the law or the facts in this case," she said. Criminal complaints in felony cases are typically reserved for more exigent circumstances, such as ongoing threats to public safety or national security. And Justice Department guidelines and norms have typically urged prosecutors to avoid taking overt investigative steps on politically sensitive cases so close to a national election. Prosecutors filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint overnight is likely to raise further questions about whether the case is politically motivated. "What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office? In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," said Floris' legal team in a statement provided to CBS News. "In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed," the lawyers said. "That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself. Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom. We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing." The charges center on testimony that Floris and Benavides gave a congressional committee on July 19, 2023 and September 28, 2023, respectively. The superseding complaint alleges the defendants "knowingly and willfully provided materially false statements to the Committee about their respective awareness of and involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden, and thereby corruptly obstructed, and impeded and endeavored to influence, obstruct, and impede the due proper administration of the law." The complaint is focused on statements they made in testimony concerning their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force, and one of its counterintelligence operations known as "Round River," which was focused on collecting derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation" ahead of the 2020 election. Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election The complaint alleges that the defendants made false statements in their testimony "for the purpose of minimizing or concealing FITF's engagement with, and communications about, the Hunter Biden investigations and to impede the Congressional investigation." articles.title: The midterms are a week away. What do the latest polls say?
articles.summary: The 2026 midterm elections are just 7 days away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is running out — and the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape is reaching its final form — and some clear polling trends have emerged. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears. Yahoo The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (3 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead (also 3 points) into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.6 points on the generic ballot. Seven days later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But with 7 days to go, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 6.9 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 9 percentage points , on average — and it has grown over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . Two new nonpartisan polls also show Jackson ahead; a Republican poll released over the weekend gives Collins a 0.5% edge. Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Ten polls have been conducted in October. Nine of them have shown El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 7 percentage points . The latest survey (for the Detroit News) puts El-Sayed ahead by 6 points . Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. But a new Echelon Insights poll shows a tie . Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by more than 10 points, on average . One of the most recent nonpartisan surveys showed him ahead by 14 . New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7 percentage points — over the last month. Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . Some September polls showed a tie, or Sullivan slightly ahead. Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 2 and 6 points. A new YouGov poll gives Talarico a 5-point lead . Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of new Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say : Marshall leads by 1 point in the latest sounding — but it's the only survey conducted over the last month that shows him ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham holds a narrow lead in recent surveys . But it is small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Thursday gave Andrews a 1-point advantage. Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20. KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 60.4% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -23.4% — near his all-time low. Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters: New York Times/Siena University : -26% American Research Group : -38% CNN/SSRS : -35% Reuters/Ipsos : -35% Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 71% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 46-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency  — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. articles.title: Supreme Court declines to restore judges' power to pause deportation cases
articles.summary: By Andrew Chung Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas ‌that bars the once-common practice. The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal ‌advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues in the dispute. The Supreme Court's decision, issued as a brief, ​one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from decision. The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal ‌government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the ⁠rule's invalidation. Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as ⁠on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction. Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty. Administrative closure has been applied over the years in ​hundreds ​of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump's ​hardline approach toward immigrants. In 2024, Biden's administration adopted a ‌regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump's first term in office that had been judicially blocked. After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge. In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens ‌illegally present in this country." Trump's administration and the state then jointly asked ​US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement ​declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O'Connor did so, blocking it ​permanently, nationwide. Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal ‌de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case ​to defend the rule, but O'Connor ​rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations. The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O'Connor's decision. The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told ​the Supreme Court in a filing that ‌Trump's administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" Texas to eliminate a regulation ​it disliked. "The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception," they ​wrote. (Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/us-supreme-court-denies-immigration-160948159.html

articles.title: FBI raids Beverly Hills mansion as part of former Rep. Eric Swalwell investigation
articles.summary: Federal agents served warrants Tuesday morning at a mansion in Beverly Hills in connection with former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell. (Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times) The FBI Tuesday morning raided a mansion in Beverly Hills in connection with an investigation into former Rep. Eric Swalwell, sources told The Times. Swalwell, a Democrat from Dublin, dropped out of the California governor’s race and resigned from Congress in April after allegations that he sexually assaulted a former staffer and acted inappropriately with other young women, which he denied at the time. Before he dropped out of the race, polls indicated that Swalwell was among the front-runners. On Tuesday, FBI agents were in Beverly Hills executing a search warrant on North Roxbury Drive in connection with the probe . “We are executing a search warrant. Court documents are sealed. No arrests are planned,” said FBI spokesperson Lourdes Arocho. The raid is taking place at the home of billionaire Stephen Cloobeck, sources confirmed to The Times. Swalwell stayed at the home several times while campaigning and used it for political events before he was kicked out in April after the allegations against him became public. In one of his last acts there, Swalwell filmed a video denying the rape and sexual assault allegations. Cloobeck, 64, is a one-time California gubernatorial candidate and a well-known figure in Democratic politics. He got rich in the timeshare industry, eventually selling his Las Vegas-based Diamond Resorts company to a private equity firm for $2.2 billion. He immersed himself in Nevada Democratic politics, growing close with the late U.S. Sen. Harry Reid, and later launched his long-shot bid for California governor. He quickly faded in the crowded field, failing to garner above 1% in any poll, and then threw his support behind Swalwell. More recently, he has found himself in the news for being embroiled in a criminal case with Adva Lavie, an OnlyFans model accused of seducing rich men for money. In August, agents seized Swalwell’s electronic devices and raided his Washington home, even briefly holding the former lawmaker at San Francisco International Airport, a person familiar with the inquiry told The Times. The source said Swalwell was held in August at SFO for search purposes and released the same day. Federal prosecutors are using civil rights law to pursue an inquiry into his conduct as a member of Congress. Authorities in New York and Los Angeles County are conducting separate investigations. His home was also searched during the summer, the source added, based on a warrant in connection with a civil rights investigation concerning the sexual assault allegations. Investigators sought to seize Swalwell’s white iPhone and MacBook Pro, according to court records. They sought the devices as part of their inquiry into whether Swalwell violated a federal law that makes it a crime for anyone acting under official government authority to willfully deprive a person of their constitutional rights, according to the court filings. Swalwell has denied any wrongdoing, but the accusations upended the California governor’s race and shook Capitol Hill, where both parties reckoned with a culture of secrecy and silence around sexual impropriety. articles.title: Gas prices under Trump are now higher on average than during Biden's time in office
articles.summary: New data from the Energy Information Administration showed that gas prices since Jan. 20, 2025 have averaged $3.458 per gallon — the first time in President Trump's second term that overall average gas prices have surpassed the average seen during President Biden's four years in office. The weekly government data, released Tuesday, shows a reading of $4.269 per gallon for Oct. 26, which nudged up the average price under Trump — from Jan. 27, 2025 to this week. It has now surpassed the $3.455-per-gallon average seen from Jan. 25, 2021, to Jan. 20, 2025. Trump's gas price record is narrowly favorable to Biden's when comparing the first 91 weekly readings of both men's presidencies. "US Regular Gasoline Prices" from Jan. 25, 2021 to Oct. 24, 2022 averaged $3.517 per gallon. Biden oversaw a spike in prices — including the highest gas prices on record of $5.006 per gallon the week of June 13, 2022 — as the US confronted oil shocks that followed Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The new numbers come exactly one week before the midterm elections and underline a clear political challenge for Trump and his party as polling shows that voters blame the president for gas price increases , which spiked immediately following the invasion of Iran earlier this year. Read more: What an extended war with Iran could mean for gas prices The gas price data also cuts against the president's message, which has been a consistent promise since the 2024 campaign to lower energy prices through new drilling. Just this past weekend at a rally in Georgia , Trump offered his oft-repeated message that high gas prices are worth it, describing them as "temporarily high." "You're still paying lower than Biden or Obama," he said. Yet gas prices in Trump's second term are now essentially equal to Biden's and are significantly higher than the $2.476 per gallon average seen during Trump's first term as well as the $2.969 per gallon average during President Obama's eight years in office, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis of the EIA data. President Donald Trump speaks to the press at Joint Base Andrews inMaryland, on Monday. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images) KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images At the Georgia rally, Trump celebrated another effect of high gas prices: bigger oil company profits. "Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East," the president said, citing increased exports of US oil at higher prices. He added that his advisers urged him not to make that point and acknowledged that bad headlines could follow, "but I said, 'I don't give a damn, I'm going to say it: We are making a freaking fortune.'" Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: Photos show Ukraine's Starlink was down during fatal strike
articles.summary: Kharkiv, Ukraine – Yulia Spichak, a 34 year-old makeup artist in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, dropped her son off at an English-language lesson on Oct. 19 and sat down in a nearby park to send a selfie to her sister, Alina. Seconds later, a Russian drone slammed into the park, killing Spichak and four others, including a 1-year-old girl. The attack came six days after Elon Musk's SpaceX throttled Ukraine's access to Starlink , which Ukraine has been using to coordinate its defenses against Russian attacks and for some of its offensive operations. In a post on X, Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by also using it for attacks on Russia. Ukrainian officials told CBS News that the restrictions imposed without advance notice affected ground-based air defense radars and drone interceptors, hindering the military's ability to stop incoming Russian strikes. "It's an essential part of the air defense infrastructure," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian member of parliament on the National Security, Defense and Intelligence Committee, told CBS News Monday. "I couldn't say that all other air defenses stopped working, no. But this part is quite essential for the defense of civilians in Ukraine." CBS News obtained photographs that show Ukraine's ground-based air defense radars' Starlink connectivity dropping to .1 megabytes per second on Oct. 19, the day of the Kharkiv drone attack. That would not be enough to load a webpage, let alone power air defense radars, according to a source familiar with the technology who requested anonymity because he was not permitted to comment on the matter. On Saturday, Ukrainian officials confirmed that Starlink's access had been restored across the country, with Musk admitting that SpaceX had throttled connectivity. "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week." Ukrainian officials have also complained of connectivity problems with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade network, which runs on the same constellation of satellites as Starlink and serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations. But Musk said the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House referred CBS News to President Trump's comments last week, during which he told reporters that he did not order the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine. Alina Spichak, the sister of Yulia, the make-up artist who died in the strike in Kharkiv, revisited the park where she died with CBS News on Sunday. She said the Geran-4 Russian jet-powered drone that killed her sister arrived so quickly the victims didn't hear it coming. "I understand that everyone has their own lives and nobody wants to look at these horrors. But I believe that the whole world has to know what is happening in Ukraine, that there is a war here and we are being attacked," Alina Spichak said. "I really hope that it will end soon." articles.title: Trump could set off a Senate showdown if a Democrat wins in Alaska
articles.summary: Senators are bracing for a potential floor fight over accepting the results of the Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) — and perhaps other battleground contests — if President Trump urges allies to dispute what he might view as unfair or “rigged” results. Democratic senators generally view Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) as a straight shooter who would be averse to rejecting an election result in an Alaska Senate race certified by the governor and lieutenant governor. But they aren’t ruling out the possibility that the president will prod his MAGA allies in the Senate to contest the election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and blames his loss on voter confusion leading to a significant number of votes for his opponent with a similar name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. If Alaska’s top officials certify Peltola as the winner, and Trump calls on Senate allies to reject that finding, it puts Thune in a tough spot and potentially sets up a messy floor fight. “Everybody is gaming everything out, and everybody is preparing for everything,” a Senate Democratic aide said of the preparations for potential Republican objections if Peltola narrowly beats the incumbent Republican senator. Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University and a Senate rules expert, said Trump’s aggressive threat to challenge a Democratic win in Alaska could lead to a nasty Senate floor fight. “We can’t rule anything out at this stage just given the president’s single-minded persistence that there’s a lot of electoral fraud conducted by Democrats,” she said. “Would he push Republicans to object to the seating, if Alaska certified the seating of Peltola? The second question is, if he did that, would Republicans actually follow through?” Binder continued. “That gets us into the hornet’s nest of what the Senate would do to challenge a literal swearing in,” she added. “There’s no single charted pathway here.” She noted that, historically, if Alaska certifies Peltola as the winner over Sen. Dan Sullivan, Republicans could object to swearing her in. “I could imagine a scenario where they would want to swear her in, and somebody objects,” she said. Senate sources familiar with how the floor process would play out said that a Trump-allied senator or a group of GOP senators could signal an intention to object to Peltola — or to the Democratic winner of another close Senate race where Trump might claim election fraud — taking the oath of office to become senator in 2027. That would then lead to a negotiation between Thune and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) over how to resolve the situation. Senate Republican sources say they’re confident that incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan will defeat Peltola next week. Recent polls show Peltola leading the GOP senator by 2 percentage points, but the race is within the margin of error. Recent surveys by Data for Progress, InsiderAdvantage and Alaska Survey Research showed the Democrat leading by 2 points while a New York Times/Siena poll conducted from Sept. 24 to Oct. 1 showed her ahead of Sullivan by 7 points. Alaska has ranked-choice voting, which could shift how some votes are counted. One relevant Senate precedent comes from January 1997, when Republican candidate Woody Jenkins petitioned the Senate to throw out Democrat Mary Landrieu’s victory in the 1996 Senate race in Louisiana. Landrieu won by more than 5,000 votes, but Jenkins alleged “widespread vote tampering.” Senate leaders resolved the matter by agreeing to seat Landrieu “without prejudice” and referring the allegations of election fraud to the Senate Rules Committee to investigate. The deal left open the door to the Senate voting to unseat Landrieu by a majority vote if the charges of cheating were substantiated. In the end, the Rules Committee voted unanimously in October 1997 to end its investigation and clear Landrieu of wrongdoing even though it acknowledged some voting irregularities. Trump is laying the groundwork for a similar fight this fall if Peltola wins, giving Democrats a crucial pickup in a GOP-leaning state. The Trump Justice Department last week asked a federal court to block the certification of the winner of the Alaska Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and could argue that he would have won if his near-namesake, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., hadn’t been on the ballot. Legal experts have broadly dismissed the Justice Department lawsuit as meritless, raising the prospect that Trump’s next move may be to demand that GOP senators refuse to seat Peltola if she wins by a small margin. “They’ve set up the argument already that there’s a deliberate deception on the part of the other Dan Sullivan, and even though this seems to have been adjudicated in Alaska law, they will certainly argue the issue of fairness remains,” said Steven S. Smith, a professor of political science at Arizona State University, who follows Senate politics. Alaska’s Division of Elections, which is led by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, initially removed “Dan J. Sullivan” from the ballot, but a state judge later ruled that he be placed back on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld that decision . To avoid confusion, the Alaska ballot lists “Dan S. Sullivan” as the Republican incumbent and lists his opponent as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without party affiliation. Given that the Alaska Supreme Court has already ruled that the little-known Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. deserves a spot on the ballot, it would be hard to see how state officials could withhold the certification of a narrow Peltola victory without being overturned by the courts, legal experts say. That then sets the stage for a fight in the Senate, where any number of Trump allies or ambitious Republican senators who are looking for a springboard for national publicity could object to seating Peltola. “This is really a question of Trump-backed Republicans, and I think with Trump probably urging them to exploit every opening, the certification of the Democrat will lead to a Republican challenge if they’re in a position in the Senate to do so,” Smith said. If Peltola wins her race by a narrow margin, however, she will need Alaska’s Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who handles the duties of the secretary of State, to certify her victory. If Republican state officials refuse to certify a Peltola victory, then Senate Republicans argue the Senate rules would not allow the upper chamber to seat her when the Senate convenes for the new Congress on Jan. 3. The matter would need to be resolved by Alaska’s courts. A similar stalemate played out in 2009 after the close contest between Democrat Al Franken and GOP Sen. Norm Coleman in Minnesota. The state’s Republican Gov. Tim Pawlenty signed the election certificate validating Franken’s victory only after the Minnesota Supreme Court unanimously ruled in June 2009 that Franken had won the race by just more than 200 votes. Democrats, who had 59 seats at the time, agreed not to seat Franken until the legal process played out. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. articles.title: Missouri voters protected abortion rights in 2024. Now they're voting on it again.
articles.summary: Just two years after Missouri voters approved an amendment enshrining the right to reproductive freedom in the state constitution, abortion, which was also protected by the measure, is on the ballot there again. On Nov. 3, Missouri residents will be voting on Amendment 3, only this time it would prohibit abortion, except in cases of medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, rape or incest. If the abortion is due to rape or incest, the procedure must occur no later than 12 weeks' gestation. Since Roe v. Wade was overruled by the Supreme Court in June 2022, 13 states have ceased nearly all abortion services while four states have a six-week ban on books, according to an ABC News tally. Missouri lawmakers move to repeal abortion protections enacted by voters Following the Supreme Court decision, Missouri enacted a trigger ban, prohibiting most abortions in the state. However, in November 2024, Missouri became the first state to overturn a near-total abortion ban through a direct vote of the people by passing Amendment 3 -- the same name as the upcoming ballot measure -- with about 52% of the vote. "Missourians have access to abortion care because the people made it possible," Mallory Schwarz, executive director of the nonprofit Abortion Action Missouri, told ABC News. "But not even months after our 2024 vote, politicians started plotting to overturn the will of the people and now, in a couple of weeks, voters will have to vote again to protect the right to abortion that we enshrined in the constitution previously." David A. Lieb/AP Photo, FILE - PHOTO: In this May 14, 2025, file photo, abortion-rights activists protest in the Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City, as the state Senate approves a proposed constitutional amendment to restrict abortion. What is Am e ndm e nt 3? Amendment 3 would repeal the 2024 amendment that granted reproductive freedom, including abortion through fetal viability, which is typically between 24 and 26 weeks' gestation. If approved, the amendment would also permit state lawmakers to enact legislation to regulate abortions and access to care. Examples include laws requiring physicians providing abortion care to have admitting privileges at a nearby hospital and licensing requirements for abortion facilities. State Sen. Adam Schnelting, who sponsored the proposal that led to Amendment 3 being placed on this year's ballot, told ABC News that passing the amendment is "critical to protecting women and children and providing Missourians with a measure that is more in line with their values than the one narrowly passed two years ago." The amendment would also prohibit gender-affirming care procedures, cross-sex hormones or puberty-blocking drugs for minors. However, gender-affirming surgeries and medical treatments for minors are already illegal in Missouri under statutory law. Opponents of the amendment have argued that including language about gender-affirming care is an attempt to mask the parts of the amendment that would limit abortion care. "What politicians are trying to do is mislead voters and overturn the will of the people and ban abortion again," Tori Schafer, an attorney for the ACLU of Missouri, told ABC News. "And they've shown they're willing to resort to all kinds of tricky tactics in order to do that." Schafer said organizations supporting Amendment 3 don't use the word "abortion" in their ads campaigning for the amendment to pass "because they know, like we know, that abortion care is popular in Missouri." Schnelting said the statutory ban on gender-affirming procedures and treatment for minors expires in 2027 and including that language in Amendment 3 would ensure such a ban is permanent. The ACLU of Missouri said the sunset clause only pertains to hormone therapy and that surgery is currently banned in Missouri. Fighting for their lives: Women and the impact of abortion restrictions in post-Roe America Possibl e cons e qu e nc e s if Am e ndm e nt 3 is pass e d After the trigger ban was passed in Missouri in 2022, the state's last abortion clinic in St. Louis was forced to stop providing such care . In 2023 alone, more than 12,000 Missouri women traveled to neighboring states, including Illinois and Kansas , to receive care, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive rights organization. Additionally, in 2025, more than 3,000 Missourians obtained medication abortions through telehealth from out-of-state clinicians, nearly four times higher than two years prior, the Guttmacher Institute found. Some abortion providers told local news outlets they were seeing patients develop complications while waiting for treatment and some patients said they'd had to flee Missouri to seek abortion care for conditions including fetal anomalies. "Missourians have lived under an abortion ban in the past," Schwarz said. "We've seen people turned away from the emergency room when they needed emergency abortion care. We've seen women forced to wait until their complication was serious enough that they were able to access care or have to flee the state to get care in another state that they should be able to get in their own community." Schwarz said Abortion Action Missouri's canvassers have had conversations with Missourians against Amendment 3 from all walks of life. One such conversation was with a Catholic voter who said they did not support abortion rights but also did not support the new amendment. "They said, 'I'm personally pro-life, but we already voted on this and I'm voting "no" this time because politicians should be listening to the people,'" Schwarz said. "'Politicians shouldn't get to overturn any vote just because they don't like it.' And so, we are hearing that [at] the doors every day, every weekend." A state-by-state breakdown of where abortion stands after ballot initiatives pass Schnelting said the response to Amendment 3 from his constituents has been largely positive and called the claims that it is overturning the will of the people a "specious argument." Anti-abortion rights groups have praised the new Amendment 3, arguing that the 2024 vote was extreme and goes beyond what Missourians have historically supported. "Despite what voters were sold before Election Day, as soon as [2024's] Amendment 3 passed, the abortion lobby brought litigation to perform late-term abortions, end parental consent and remove every safety regulation on their industry," Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said in a statement last year. "Amendment 3 is far too extreme and dangerous." Missouri is not the only state with abortion on the ballot on Nov. 3. Voters in three states -- Idaho, Nevada and Virginia -- will consider measures to protect abortion rights and, in some cases, reproductive freedom. Schafer, from ACLU of Missouri, said other states can learn from Missouri about how access to abortion can be at risk even after voters vote to protect care. "While this fight is really important to folks like me who live in Missouri and have to suffer the consequences of our legislature ignoring the will of the people, we know that this campaign will also impact folks all across the country," Schafer said. "We have friends in other states who have passed their own versions of the right to reproductive freedom, and we don't want this attempt by our legislature to embolden this opposition strategy across the country." She went on, "So we know that a lot of eyes are on Missouri, and Missourians deeply believe in the right to make their own decisions free from political interference." articles.title: Israel votes today, but it could take months to determine who wins
articles.summary: Polling stations in Israel will close on Tuesday evening, but it could be weeks before Benjamin Netanyahu or one of his opponents will be declared the next prime minister. It might even require another election . That's because Israelis vote for parties and not candidates. None of the several main parties is expected to win anywhere close to a 61-seat majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset. So the next prime minister will have to cobble together a coalition. Polls show a tight race between coalitions supporting Netanyahu and his main opponent, retired Gen. Gadi Eisenkot . In the end, both could fall short of a 61-seat majority, meaning another election would be held in the coming months with Netanyahu's government staying on as a caretaker. Here's a look at the process. Israeli broadcasters release exit polls Shortly after polls close at 10 p.m. local time (2000 GMT), Israel's three main television broadcasters will release exit polls estimating how many seats were won by each party. The exit polls usually provide a good indication of how people have voted. But they also could vary and may not be borne out by the official results, which will be released in the coming days. The Associated Press calls thousands of elections in the United States, but doesn't declare winners in foreign elections. Party leaders negotiate If, as expected, neither coalition pulls off a clear victory, then the coming weeks will see intense negotiations and bargaining among party leaders as they try to get to 61 seats. Israel's largely ceremonial president, Isaac Herzog, will hold consultations with all the party leaders after the election and ask the candidate who appears most likely to form a coalition to do so. If that candidate is unable to assemble a majority within a maximum of six weeks, then others could be given a shot. The process gives outsized power to smaller parties that can often provide a crucial margin. The leaders of the bigger parties typically woo them with promises of Cabinet positions, budgets or specific policies. This election could in theory be decided by Arab-led parties . Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far ruled out any partnership with them. But they could allow Eisenkot to form a minority government by backing him from outside the coalition or even just abstaining from the Knesset vote to seat the next government. Gridlock would lead to another election If, after all the negotiations, no one is able to form a majority, a new election would be held in the next few months and the process would repeat itself. Netanyahu's government would remain as a caretaker and public services wouldn't be affected. But it would lack the authority to enact major policy changes. Even another election may not resolve matters. The last national election held in Israel, in November 2022, was the fifth in 3½ years. ___ This story has been corrected to show that polls close at 2000 GMT, not 1900 GMT. articles.title: Trump-backed senator warns Republicans could lose the Senate over 1 state
articles.summary: WICHITA, Kan. — Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., knows that he’s running for his political life, even in deep-red Kansas, where a Democrat hasn’t won since the Great Depression. It’s a Senate race that, until just a few months ago, was not on national Republicans’ radar. But Adam Hamilton, a well-known megachurch pastor styling himself as a moderate, has made the race uncomfortably close for Marshall and the GOP and pushed what was once a safe bet into toss-up territory. In an interview with Fox News Digital in Wichita, Kan., hours before President Donald Trump was set to rally behind the embattled incumbent, Marshall acknowledged that if he falls, Democrats may very well gain control of the Senate. Sleeper Senate Race Emerges As Unexpected Headache For Republicans Ahead Of Midterms President Donald Trump and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., attend a campaign event in Park City, Kansas, on Oct. 19, 2026. "I think that, you know, I'm not a political expert, I'm a physician, but if we lose Kansas, I don't see how we keep control of the Senate," Marshall said. "And that's why a vote for Adam Hamilton is a vote for Chuck Schumer and Democrat control of the Senate. It’s that simple." Republicans are trying to maintain, and even grow, their slim, 53-seat majority in the upper chamber. Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, wasn’t supposed to be a problem. Read On The Fox News App But political experts on the ground contend that Hamilton’s uniqueness as a candidate — he’s been a prominent figure in Kansas for roughly three decades leading the massive Church of the Resurrection — and the political headwinds associated with Trump have created an ideal environment for Marshall to lose. "I can't imagine how factors could be any better for Democrats than they are this election cycle," Don Haider-Markel, a professor of political science at the University of Kansas, told Fox News Digital. "The last time it seemed to be close at all was 2020, and that race ended up not being as close." Dem Senate Hopeful Rejects Schumer But Benefits From Millions In Spending By His Allies That was Marshall’s first race for the Senate, where he won by nearly 12 points with Trump at the top of the ticket. But as Haider-Markel and others have pointed out, midterm elections are typically a check on the party in power, and Trump is not on the ballot this year, though that’s a reality he implored Kansans to ignore during his rally in Park City, Kansas. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend please that I'm on the ballot," Trump said. "Just pretend." Still, voters in Kansas are dealing with affordability issues and high fuel prices , a point that Marshall admitted was why his race was much closer than outside observers initially predicted. "Look, it's the price of gas, and I do feel people's pain," Marshall said. "Every year I go to all 105 counties, finish up the 105 counties in June, and as that price of gas went up, I felt more and more frustration." "So maybe we're up 12 points before the Iran war, and as the price went up our poll numbers went down, so I think it's the price of gas," he continued. Along the asphalt and concrete arteries that connect Hamilton’s home base of Overland Park, Kansas, to what would be, for a brief moment, the center of the MAGA universe in Wichita, neon signs sprouting from gas stations almost all showed fuel prices that hovered just below $4 for gas and well over $6 for diesel . Trump Voters Reveal Their Biggest Fear Heading Into Midterms — And It's Not Rising Prices Democrat senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton answers questions from the media after a televised debate with Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., at WDAF studios in Kansas City, Mo. Nathaniel Birkhead, a professor of political science at Kansas State University, argued that high gas and diesel prices were certainly a contributing factor to Marshall’s struggles, but not the only one. Birkhead told Fox News Digital that it was Marshall’s tight connection to Trump at a time when the "Trump Brand is not particularly popular" has left an opening for a Democrat like Hamilton to enter the fray. "So we have this kind of contrast of Hamilton benefiting from kind of a down year for Republicans. But then also, again, the fact that Marshall is really kind of tying himself to Trump rather than trying to kind of separate himself," Birkhead said. "I think if this had been Jerry Moran running instead of Roger Marshall, I think it'd be far less competitive." Click Here To Download The Fox News App Therein lies the conundrum for Marshall and Republicans — they know that they need Trump’s support and his loyal base of voters, but they have to walk a fine line to capture other Republican voters and independents that might sit this election out or vote the other way. And that’s the crux of Marshall’s argument: without MAGA voters, he can’t win. "Look, I'm the doctor always weighing the benefits and risks of everything. And I'm telling you, we don't win this election without Trump voters getting out and voting," Marshall said. "The majority of the undecideds are Trump supporters. And they need to hear from him, 'Here's the plan, and this is how we're going to bring those prices back down, that if we leave Democrats in control, the price of the gas will never go down.'" articles.title: 三季度收入近乎腰斩，泡泡玛特把增长预期押给回头客
articles.summary: 市场等待已久的泡泡玛特三季报，终于揭晓了去年全球爆红之后的业绩回落幅度。 10月27日，泡泡玛特披露第三季度未经审计的经营数据，整体收入同比下降45%—50%。 其中，中国市场下降25%—30%，亚太下降65%—70%，美洲下降70%—75%，欧洲及其他地区下降50%—55%。 国内线上线下渠道也出现明显分化：线下收入同比下降5%—10%，线上收入则下降45%—50%。 尽管市场此前已普遍预期泡泡玛特将在去年同期的极高基数下出现收入下滑，实际表现仍比部分机构下调后的预测更加疲弱。 相比收入降幅，管理层更强调业务已经出现的企稳迹象。 在当天的业绩交流会上，泡泡玛特首席运营官司德表示， 海外业务经历年初以来的持续回落后，第三季度大部分国家和地区已经趋于平稳，第四季度有望在传统销售旺季实现环比增长。中国市场全年则预计仍能实现同比正增长。 但销售企稳与重回增长之间，仍然存在距离。 去年，LABUBU的全球热度推动泡泡玛特快速获取海外消费者，大量需求集中在线上释放。 而在此次业绩会上，如何提高门店经营效率、推动会员持续消费，以及改善全球商品与库存管理，成为管理层反复讨论的问题。 LABUBU让泡泡玛特一夜爆红，接下来的增长，要看它能留下多少回头客。 增长预期的两面 泡泡玛特管理层对中国市场全年正增长的预期，实际需要跨越的门槛并不高。 2025年，泡泡玛特中国市场收入208.52亿元。今年上半年，中国市场已实现122.01亿元收入，同比增长47.3%，为全年增长积累了较大优势。 据此估算，即使今年下半年同比下降约31%，中国市场全年仍可保持正增长。 从具体经营指标来看，泡泡玛特国内消费者基础仍表现出一定韧性。 管理层透露，第三季度中国线下门店客流保持正增长，品牌新客同比实现双位数增长，绝对人数环比第二季度也有所增加。 截至第三季度，中国内地会员次复购水平与去年同期基本持平，次年留存率有所提高。单看第三季度，跨IP消费的老客人数仍保持较高的双位数增长。 这些数据与线上收入接近腰斩的表现形成反差。此前受到热门IP带动的线上集中购买明显回落，但已经进入品牌体系的消费者，仍然保持了一定的购买活跃度。 海外市场的情况则更为复杂。 2025年第三季度是泡泡玛特历史上销售额最高的季度，尤其在美洲和亚太地区，LABUBU带来的集中购买推动收入快速增长。 今年同期，公司面对的是极高的比较基数，以及线上流量持续回落的压力。 司德表示，直到第三季度，海外大多数国家和地区的流量才基本趋于平稳。相比线下门店，线上渠道的恢复仍然缓慢。 他解释，去年海外销售爆发时，线下网络尚未充分铺开，大量销售集中在线上。如今，公司更多通过线下门店获取新客、积累会员，再逐步引导消费者进入线上渠道，这也意味着线上恢复可能需要更长时间。 从乐观的角度看，如果海外销售已在第三季度接近阶段性低点，第四季度旺季、新品供应和门店经营改善，有望推动收入环比回升。随着去年异常高的销售基数逐步消化，明年的同比增长压力也可能减轻。 但另一种可能是，去年海外市场的部分爆款需求具有较强的一次性特征。即使流量企稳，新的日常销售规模仍然可能明显低于去年。 这意味着，第四季度收入环比反弹，并不必然代表海外业务已经重新建立持续增长能力。 在海外扩张成本持续增加、销售前景仍不明朗的情况下，泡泡玛特开始更加审慎地评估新店，同时将经营重心更多放在已有门店和消费者身上。 经营海外回头客 相比经营多年的中国市场，泡泡玛特海外会员体系还有明显的提升空间。 中国业务负责人褚音在三季度业绩会上透露，目前亚太市场跨渠道消费占比不足中国内地的三分之一，会员销售占比也存在较大差距。 跨渠道消费反映的是消费者在不同销售渠道之间的流转购买情况。例如，最初在线下门店购买商品的消费者，之后又通过线上官方渠道购买其他产品。 虽然这一指标不直接等同于复购率，但能反映线上线下共同经营消费者的程度。 对于泡泡玛特而言，去年通过LABUBU认识品牌、完成首次购买的海外消费者，能否继续购买其他IP、形成跨渠道消费习惯，是下一阶段值得挖掘的增长空间。 目前，泡泡玛特已在全球绝大多数市场建立会员系统，并将线下门店会员拉新纳入日常经营考核。但从系统覆盖到消费者形成稳定的购物习惯，仍需要持续运营。 今年下半年，中国业务负责人褚音进一步接手亚太区管理。管理层解释，这一调整旨在加强中国与亚太团队的交流配合，让中国团队更了解海外市场，同时帮助亚太提升长期经营能力。 这一调整背后，是泡泡玛特全球管理模式的变化。 早期海外业务规模较小时，各市场拥有较大的经营自主权。随着规模扩大，公司近两年持续调整管理架构，亚太业务先后由文德一、司德统筹，如今进一步引入中国业务团队的运营经验。 亚太业务覆盖约十个国家和地区，不同市场的消费需求、渠道结构存在差异，总部与各国团队之间也有大量协调工作。 褚音表示，接手后，亚太团队开始简化业务流程，加强总部与各国管理人员之间的协作，并引入具有国际品牌运营经验的人才。 组织协同之外，亚太的商品和渠道管理也开始向精细化转变。 去年LABUBU热销期间，区域团队更多关注热门IP的销售表现。 如今，亚太开始借鉴中国市场的运营经验，将商品管理细化至具体品类和SKU，根据不同市场的销售情况动态调整商品供给。 渠道方面，亚太团队正在减少部分国家小型线上平台的重复投入，将资源集中到运营效率更高的渠道，同时加强线上线下经营节奏的协同。 褚音强调，中国市场积累的经验不会被全盘复制，亚太仍需结合当地消费者需求与文化差异进行调整。 去年LABUBU在亚太销售中占比较高，如今公司开始更注重多IP经营。今年第三季度，亚太已有六个IP合计贡献超过60%的销售额，为消费者购买不同IP提供了更多选择。 在司德看来，海外市场接下来的增长，需要重新回到一家家普通门店的经营。 他在业绩会上举例，意大利罗马一家位于本地居民购物中心的门店，面积约180平方米，月销售额约100多万元人民币，利润率尚可。这样的成绩并不突出，却更接近泡泡玛特过去在中国市场熟悉的经营方式。 通过改善商品组合、门店服务和营销活动，持续积累当地消费者与品牌粉丝，司德希望未来将这家门店的月销售额逐步提高至150万元、180万元，甚至200万元。 从抢货到管货 上半年一度引发市场关注的库存压力，在第三季度出现了新的变化。 泡泡玛特管理层在业绩会上表示，集团库存于5月达到较高水平，从8月开始下降，到9月底已经呈现较明显的下降趋势。 不过，公司暂时不会通过大规模促销消化库存，以避免影响品牌价格体系和盈利能力。 相比库存余额的下降，更值得关注的是泡泡玛特正在重新调整全球商品采购与调配机制。 司德透露，今年泡泡玛特在总部成立了统一管理全球采购的商品团队。 此前，全球四个区域分别判断需求、安排采购，热门IP销售火爆时，各地可能同时增加备货；当不同市场销售进度出现差异，集团则需要协调各地的商品供给。 如今，总部开始统一调控各区域采购需求，并提高跨区域商品调拨频率。 与此同时，公司根据具体SKU在不同市场和渠道的销售情况动态调整补货，不再等到初次分配的商品接近售罄后才采取行动。 这一机制既要避免不同区域重复备货，也要减少部分市场库存积压、另一些市场商品短缺的情况，提高现有库存的利用效率。 对于已经形成的库存，公司也在拓展销售渠道。 管理层透露，美国开始尝试与大型连锁零售商合作，一方面销售大版权商品，另一方面消化部分库存；亚太市场则通过拓展分销渠道和阶段性促销活动推动销售。 但更精细的商品调配，仍然无法完全解决海外供应链的交付周期问题。 目前，泡泡玛特的主要生产基地仍在中国。虽然公司已在越南探索生产三年多，但面向欧美市场的物流时效仍不如中国；公司也曾小规模探索墨西哥生产，但目前尚未看到将其发展为主要生产基地的可行路径。 司德坦言，调整生产地难以解决海外交付周期问题，公司仍需通过提前预测、排产及滚动发货，结合空运、海运和铁路运输平衡时效与成本。 尽管美国电商已实现本土发货，欧洲也在推进本土履约，但这只能改善末端配送效率，无法缩短商品进入海外仓库前的运输周期。 因此，海外业务仍依赖提前备货，需求预测偏差可能再次带来库存压力。而库存下降，也不意味着盈利能力能够同步恢复。 管理层预计，下半年毛利率较上半年下降不超过2个百分点，主要受到高毛利率海外业务收入占比下降，以及美国部分产品重新定价等因素影响。 与此同时，欧美市场持续开店推高人力、租金及装修摊销等费用，管理层预计下半年费用率上升，利润率进一步承压。 过去，热门商品集中放量可以迅速摊薄渠道及运营成本。如今，海外需求趋于平稳，已有库存和持续增加的门店成本，都需要更稳定的销售收入来消化。 如何在控制库存风险的同时提高商品周转和单店产出，正成为泡泡玛特海外业务恢复盈利能力的重要考验。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 芒果超媒前三季度净利下滑近八成，AIGC新故事尚待兑现
articles.summary: 作为AIGC影视领域最受关注的上市公司之一，芒果超媒尚未从AI内容业务中获得可量化的业绩增长。 10月27日，芒果超媒披露2026年三季报。第三季度，公司实现营收31.58亿元，同比增长1.87%；归母净利润仅1155.19万元，同比下降95.42%。 前三季度，公司营收93.51亿元，同比增长3.18%；归母净利润2.13亿元，同比下降79.01%。 业绩表现与近期股价走势形成鲜明反差。 随着AI影视、短剧等概念受到市场关注，芒果超媒股价自8月底开始反弹，10月9日一度20%涨停。截至10月27日，公司股价收于23.48元，较9月中旬上涨约38%。 资本市场已经开始关注芒果超媒的AI内容业务，但传统业务的盈利压力仍未缓解。 公司将前三季度利润下滑归因于会员收入下降、内容成本刚性，以及投资标的公允价值变动等因素。 其中，会员业务是影响盈利表现的重要因素。 芒果超媒解释，部分渠道端合作模式调整，以及重点影视剧排播节奏变化，导致会员收入同比下降。 对于长视频平台而言，会员收入与优质内容供给密切相关，但影视剧采购和自制内容投入又具有一定刚性。即使收入减少，相关成本也难以同步下降。 这种压力已经反映在利润表中。 前三季度，芒果超媒营业成本同比增长11.8%，明显超过营收增速，综合毛利率从上年同期的约26.9%降至20.8%。 尽管第三季度毛利率较第二季度环比提升5.45个百分点，但仍未改变累计盈利承压的局面。 投资业务进一步放大了利润降幅。前三季度，公司确认投资项目公允价值变动损失约1.26亿元，信用减值损失约8831万元。 同期，公司利润总额已转为亏损2149万元，由于确认约2.37亿元所得税收益，最终实现归母净利润2.13亿元。 利润大幅下滑，也让芒果超媒寻找新内容生产方式的紧迫性更加突出。 长期以来，长视频平台依靠持续投入优质剧综吸引会员和广告主，但制作周期长、成本高，单部作品的商业回报又存在较大不确定性。当会员收入增长放缓，内容成本难以同步压缩，传统经营模式便面临更大压力。 生成式AI为这一困境提供了新的解决思路。通过降低部分场景制作、拍摄及后期环节的成本，AI有望让平台以更低投入生产更多内容，减少对高成本项目的依赖。 芒果超媒正在将这一探索提升至战略层面。 在此次三季报中，公司用了较大篇幅介绍AIGC业务，并将其视为探索第二条内容供给曲线的重要方向。 今年以来，芒果超媒设立AIGC创新内容中心和AI产业化中心，依托芒果大模型、芒果灵创AIGC内容生产平台，推动人工智能进入内容策划、创制和生产全流程。 其中，AI长剧《后西游记》已登陆卫视黄金档。芒果超媒在财报中表示，该项目已跑通商业化链路，标志着公司在AI精品内容领域实现从零到一的突破。 在此基础上，芒果TV推出AIGC内容厂牌“灵创剧场”，重点布局精品女频中长剧、国风经典IP焕新和少儿动画三个方向，尝试将AI内容从单个项目探索扩展为系列化供给。 这一布局意味着，芒果超媒希望AI不仅服务于传统内容制作，还能形成一套新的内容生产体系。 不过，从技术探索走向可持续的商业增长，仍有距离。 目前，芒果超媒尚未单独披露AIGC业务的收入、利润及制作成本，也没有提供AI改善整体内容成本结构的具体数据。 与此同时，传统内容投入仍在持续。三季报显示，公司剧集储备接近百部，存货较年初增长31.92%，主要由于影视剧集储备增加。 AIGC已经成为芒果超媒重要的战略方向，但能否从单个项目的商业化尝试，发展为持续贡献收入和利润的新业务，仍有待验证。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 飞科电器三季度净利增长27%，以高速吹风机新品拓展中高端市场
articles.summary: 飞科电器的收入增长，在第三季度重新提速。 10月27日，飞科电器披露2026年第三季度报告。公司第三季度实现营业收入10.46亿元，同比增长13.19%；归母净利润1.73亿元，同比增长26.89%；扣非净利润1.59亿元，同比增长40.82%。 这一表现带动累计收入转为增长。前三季度，公司营收30.66亿元，同比增长0.84%；归母净利润5.32亿元，同比增长16.40%；扣非净利润4.97亿元，同比增长21.95%。相比上半年营收下降4.56%、归母净利润增长11.95%，第三季度收入和利润均有所提速。 利润改善的基础，可以从成本端看到。根据三季报与半年报测算，飞科第三季度毛利率约为59.60%，较上年同期的56.10%提高约3.50个百分点。同期销售费用约3.52亿元，同比增长14.22%，收入恢复增长及毛利率提升，为营销投入增加提供了支撑。 这与上半年的经营节奏有所不同。公司此前曾解释，上半年调整运营策略和费用规划，促销费、体验店费用有所减少。到了第三季度，公司在报告中将扣非净利润增长的主要原因归结为销售收入增加。 产品端，高速吹风机是飞科拓展中高端市场的重要方向。公司在半年报中披露，今年推出智能变温高速吹风机，延续此前“银河星环”高速电吹风等产品的布局。剃须刀则围绕便携、智能感应及高速往复式等功能迭代，针对年轻消费者对外观设计和使用体验的需求更新产品。 这些新品承接的是飞科与博锐两个品牌的不同任务。飞科通过技术和设计升级拓展中高端客群，博锐则强调性价比，继续覆盖价格敏感人群和下沉市场。同样是剃须刀、电吹风，公司希望用不同品牌覆盖更宽的消费价格带。 从上半年的销售结构看，两个品牌的调整仍在进行。中高端产品销售占比为55.32%，同比下降1.05个百分点；博锐销售额占比则升至24.92%，同比提高5.44个百分点。中高端新品持续推出的同时，性价比产品在公司收入中的分量也在增加。 渠道上，公司上半年继续扩展、升级线下体验店及品牌形象终端，并通过抖音直播、京东到家、淘宝闪购、美团等平台导流。对剃须刀和吹风机而言，门店承担产品体验，即时零售连接附近消费者，销售场景也由传统商超和电商货架延伸至本地配送。 飞科拓展中高端市场的动作，因而同时落在产品和终端，一端用功能、设计提升产品吸引力，另一端让消费者更容易体验和购买。博锐则以较低的购买门槛承接另一部分需求。 现金流方面，前三季度公司经营活动现金净流入6.24亿元，高于同期归母净利润，但同比下降16.29%。其中第三季度净流入1.12亿元，同比下降59.15%，公司解释，主要是当季支付的采购款增加。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 市场分化传导险企利润表，招商仁和人寿三季度盈利承压
articles.summary: 利润承压、净资产回升，招商仁和人寿率先披露的业绩，折射出寿险业在市场分化下的共同考验。 10月27日，招商仁和人寿披露，公司第三季度实现净利润约0.66亿元，较第二季度减少约3.02亿元，降幅超八成； 但正是同一个季度，该公司的净资产由102.76亿元增至106.63亿元，增加约3.87亿元。 这组反差，让市场波动对险企的影响有了更具体的呈现。 一部分投资资产的估值损失压低了当期利润，另一部分资产的升值则通过其他综合收益支撑净资产，持仓结构与会计分类，共同影响着同一家公司交出的成绩单。 国泰海通证券非银行金融研究首席分析师刘欣琦判断，权益市场波动叠加上年同期高基数，将使上市险企利润承压，红利资产修复有望支持部分险企净资产增长。 招商仁和人寿为观察这一行业趋势提供了先行样本，沿着利润变化追踪，该公司净资产增长的来源也逐渐显现。 公允价值变动拖累盈利 第三季度，招商仁和人寿的利息收入约6.25亿元、投资收益约4.41亿元，合计10.66亿元；保险服务收入扣除保险服务费用、分出保费分摊，再加回摊回保险服务费用后的净额约2亿元。 利息、投资和保险服务仍构成当季利润的基本支撑； 其中，利息收入与投资收益合计略高于上半年季度平均的10.36亿元，保险服务相关净额也高于上半年季度平均的1.23亿元。 但这些收入带来的盈利贡献，受到公允价值变动损失的侵蚀。 上半年，公司公允价值变动收益为正4776万元，前三季度累计则转为损失2.80亿元。 第三季度单季公允价值变动损失由此达到约3.27亿元，对当季利润形成明显拖累。这笔损失的规模，已接近第三季度净利润环比减少额。 利息、投资收益及保险服务仍提供着收入，计入当期损益的部分金融资产却出现较大估值损失，削弱了这些收入对利润的贡献。 这一压力与当季权益市场调整相呼应。 第三季度，沪深300指数下跌12.5%，中证500指数下跌17.7%；前期强势的科技成长板块回调，高股息板块则出现修复，中证红利指数上涨9.4%。 市场调整中，部分资产仍取得正向收益。 对险企而言，持仓的差异影响投资表现，会计分类则决定这些估值变化体现在哪张报表中。 招商仁和人寿也呈现出这样的分化，第三季度，该公司计入其他综合收益的权益工具公允价值变动为正，与利润表中的估值损失形成反差。 这部分收益直接影响净资产，也将分析的视线引向了利润表之外。 净资产持续增长 以公允价值计量且其变动计入当期损益的金融资产（TPL），估值涨跌直接影响当期利润；以公允价值计量且其变动计入其他综合收益的金融资产（OCI），相关估值变化通过其他综合收益影响净资产。 截至9月末，招商仁和人寿金融投资账面余额为930.62亿元。 其中，TPL账户下的交易性金融资产为68.30亿元，占金融投资的7.34%； OCI账户下的其他债权投资为575.62亿元，其他权益工具投资为97.85亿元，二者合计673.46亿元，占金融投资的72.37%。 这意味着，公司较大部分金融投资的公允价值变化，通过OCI账户反映在净资产中。 第三季度，OCI账户下其他权益工具投资的公允价值变动贡献约9.66亿元，其他债权投资的公允价值变动贡献约3.62亿元，两项合计约13.28亿元，为当季净资产增长提供了支撑。 红利配置，为理解其中的权益资产表现提供了一条线索。 从公开持仓记录看，2023年末，招商仁和人寿旗下“传统产品3号”持有陕西煤业5143.95万股，占其总股本的0.53%，进入前十大股东名单。 2024年末，公司旗下多个产品账户也出现在汇添富中证银行ETF的主要持有人名单中，其中“分红产品4号”和“传统产品3号”分别持有约2.94亿份、2.55亿份。 这些持仓与公司的配置取向相互印证。 联合资信2025年跟踪评级报告指出，招商仁和人寿2024年权益投资规模及占比上升，原因包括根据市场情况增配高分红蓝筹股票。 煤炭个股、银行ETF的历史持仓，与增配高分红蓝筹股的投资方向相互印证，呈现出公司的红利配置基础，三季度高股息板块修复，为这一配置方向提供了有利的市场环境。 回到报表，OCI账户中的正向估值收益，是理解净资产增长的关键。 净利润只是净资产变动的一个来源，计入其他综合收益的资产和负债变化，同样会增加或减少净资产。 第三季度，招商仁和人寿净资产增加约3.87亿元，其中约0.66亿元来自当季净利润，另外约3.21亿元来自其他综合收益。 也就是说，推动当季净资产增长的主要力量，体现在利润表的净利润之外。 这3.21亿元，是资产与保险负债两端变化共同作用的结果。 当季，OCI账户下的权益和债权投资合计贡献约13.28亿元公允价值变动收益； 与此同时，计入其他综合收益的保险合同金融变动约为负10.37亿元，抵减了大部分资产端增值。综合分出再保险合同等项目后，最终形成约3.21亿元其他综合收益。 利润表中的估值压力，并未阻断招商仁和人寿当季的资本积累，OCI账户中的资产增值在抵减保险负债端的金融变动后，仍为净资产增长提供了主要支撑。 但这份率先披露的成绩单，已经映照出寿险业三季度面临的共同考验。 权益市场冷暖分化，既考验投资组合的配置，也考验资产收益与长期保单责任的匹配；随着更多险企披露业绩，各家公司在利润之外积累了多少资本，将成为观察经营成色的另一条线索。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 血制品行业承压后，上海莱士加码押注创新药
articles.summary: 10月27日晚，上海莱士披露2026年三季报。第三季度实现营业收入17.35亿元，同比下降18.9%；同期归母净利润为3.18亿元，同比下降27.93%。 承压的不止上海莱士。同为血液制品企业的派林生物，第三季度实现营业收入5.73亿元，同比下降9.24%；归母净利润为6600.31万元，同比下降45.63%。 血液制品行业正在经历一轮调整。今年以来，随着集采持续推进、市场供给增加，行业产品价格面临下行压力。 上海莱士在财报中坦言，行业渠道库存处于高位，公司主动放弃以价换量和追求发货规模，转而以终端实际销售为导向，短期内对收入及利润形成压力。 不过，上海莱士称，前三季度自产血液制品累计终端动销量同比实现两位数增长，渠道库存有所回落。 在传统业务承压之际，上海莱士正尝试通过创新药寻找新的增长空间。 9月，上海莱士血友病创新药SR604用于预防出血的Ⅲ期临床试验完成登记，正式进入确证性临床研究阶段。 据上海莱士披露，SR604是全球首个靶向活化蛋白C（APC）的血友病单抗药物，目前全球尚无同靶点产品获批上市。 血友病治疗市场具有一定增长空间。弗若斯特沙利文此前预测，到2030年，中国血友病药物市场规模有望达到141亿元。 为推进创新药产业化，上海莱士还于9月签署协议，拟收购勃林格殷格翰生物药业（中国）有限公司100%股权，获得其位于上海张江的生物制药生产基地。 该基地具备6000升规模的商业化生产能力，有望为SR604后续的临床样品制备及商业化生产提供支持。 不过，创新药从临床研究走向商业化仍需要时间，期间还面临临床试验、审批及市场竞争等不确定性。 对于上海莱士而言，创新药能否成为新的增长引擎仍有待验证，传统血液制品业务何时回暖才是当前提振业绩最直接的考验。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 五粮液三季度净利下滑48%，旺季过后需求压力重新显形
articles.summary: 白酒市场的需求压力，再次反映在五粮液的业绩中。 10月27日，五粮液披露2026年三季报。第三季度，公司实现营业收入44.42亿元，同比下降37.68%；归母净利润9.58亿元，同比下降48.25%。 这一表现与上半年形成明显反差。今年上半年，五粮液营收和归母净利润分别同比增长20.87%、89.30%。但进入第三季度，此前的增长势头未能延续，收入和利润均出现双位数下滑。 五粮液在财报中解释，市场需求偏弱，相关产品销量减少，是第三季度收入、利润下降的主要原因。 实际上，五粮液从去年就已经进入深度调整期。 2025年，受白酒消费场景收缩、市场竞争加剧等因素影响，五粮液销售量同比减少30.26%，库存量增长45.18%。 今年4月，五粮液又对2025年财务数据作出大幅更正。公司解释，基于对业务模式的梳理及谨慎性原则，调整了部分业务的收入确认核算。 调整后，五粮液2025年全年营收为405.29亿元，同比下降54.55%；归母净利润89.54亿元，同比下降71.89%。 去年的业绩大幅下滑，为今年的同比增长提供了较低的比较基数。 今年前三季度，五粮液归母净利润同比增长49.98%。公司解释，除去年同期基数较低外，今年元春旺季核心产品动销较好，也对业绩形成支撑。 只是随着旺季结束，第三季度产品销量减少，前期的增长势头未能延续。 与此同时，五粮液仍在加大市场投入。第三季度，公司销售费用约14.76亿元，同比增长19.6%。尽管投入增速放缓，但同期收入下降37.68%，销售费用与收入走势仍然背离。 前三季度，五粮液累计销售费用同比增长64.7%，持续增加的市场投入尚未扭转销量下滑的局面。 另一方面，五粮液的现金回流节奏也在发生变化。 今年上半年，公司经营活动现金流量净额为负21.54亿元，较上年同期的311.37亿元大幅减少。 前三季度虽然转正，但净额仅4668万元，同比下降99.83%。尽管利润表仍保持增长，五粮液从经营活动中实际获得的净现金已大幅减少。 五粮液在中报和三季报中均作出相同解释：一方面是上年同期基数较高，另一方面，公司根据市场变化调整了收款政策，导致收到的现金减少，银行承兑汇票到期额度同比也有所下降。 过去，头部酒企依靠经销商先款后货的结算方式，能够提前获得较为充裕的经营现金流。而在需求偏弱的市场环境中，厂家需要重新平衡产品销售、渠道资金压力和自身现金回款节奏。 目前，五粮液仍持有超过1100亿元货币资金。但在市场需求偏弱的情况下，增加销售投入和调整回款政策能否推动产品动销持续改善，仍有待观察。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 首批主动ETF募集火爆：9只提前结募，8家机构自购加码
articles.summary: 国内首批主动ETF传出募集“佳音”，市场认购热度超预期，九只产品先后售罄。 据悉，此次首批发行的18只ETF中，已有9只触及20亿元募集上限、提前结束募集并实施末日比例配售。这个幅度超出市场预期。 同时，工银瑞信等8家机构相继发布公告，以自有资金加码管理的主动ETF，也进一步强化了市场信心。 创新产品受到欢迎 此次主动ETF，之所以能受到市场欢迎，除了主动管理交易型开放式证券投资基金——这个创新品类外，各家公司高度重视，推出重磅资源支持也是关键。 据悉，与过往传统的全面跟踪指数的被动ETF不同，主动ETF是由基金经理主动选股，追求超额收益，同时又保留被动ETF可实时交易、持仓透明等核心优势的产品。 同时，为了尽力确保首批主动ETF“开门大吉”，18家产品在今年10月19日集中注册获批，并统一于10月23日开启认购。同时，可能为稳妥推进创新试点，这批产品普遍设置20亿元的募集规模上限，并配套持仓分散等风控要求，兼顾产品创新与投资者获得较好的管理安排。 9只产品公告提前结募 作为国内公募行业新品种，此次18只首批主动ETF一经开售便点燃了市场热情。 全市场的募集首日，易方达品质均衡主动管理ETF、摩根大盘成长主动管理ETF、富国价值优选量化选股主动管理ETF三只产品便率先触及20亿元募集上限，公告提前结束募集。 本周一，募集期的第二个交易日，热度继续保持，华夏质量甄选主动管理ETF、华泰柏瑞价值精选主动管理ETF、南方均衡配置主动管理ETF、平安红利景气主动管理ETF等四只产品也集中官宣提前结募。 第三天（10月27日），天弘均衡量化选股主动管理ETF、大成红利智选主动ETF也集中官宣提前结募。 至此，三天就有九只主动ETF完成募集，速度大大胜于前期预期。 后续进程须观察 公开披露公告显示，9只产品有效认购申请均采用“末日比例确认”的原则予以部分确认，未确认部分的认购款项将由销售机构退还给投资者，这或许会构成又一轮的认购潮。 剩余9只产品则仍按原定发售时间表正常推募集，后续是否触发上限、加入提前结募行列，有待观察。 另一个，可以预判的后续是，配售结束后，基金公司将发行末日比例确认公告、验资备案并披露基金成立公告，随即进入建仓期。由于此次产品的火爆程度非同一般，市场普遍预期会较快节奏完成建仓，这亦大大有利于后期市场表现 不少机构持续加码 工银瑞信基金10月24日发布公告，基于对中国资本市场长期健康稳定发展的信心，工银瑞信将运用固有资金1亿元投资工银红利主动ETF，并承诺持有期限不低于1年。 该笔投资最终确认结果以基金注册登记机构核算为准，资金将在基金认购阶段及上市之后分批落地。 工银瑞信加入后，截至目前已有8家机构加入自有资金投资主动ETF。 此前，易方达、富国、华夏、汇添富四家公司于10月22日同步公告，各出资2亿元自购旗下主动 ETF；同日，华安基金宣布出资1亿元跟进；国泰海通证券23日公告，拟投入不超过6.7亿元布局多只首批主动 ETF；20日，摩根基金公告其股东将通过摩根资产管理（亚太）出资约5亿元，相关投资将在基金上市后开展。 从现在看，各家主动ETF的管理人，各自推出了跟进、认购的措施，都进一步加快了上述进程。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
